claim: HP1α, HP1β, and HP1γ display rapid on-off dynamics in mammalian heterochromatin.
source: In mammals, HP1-mediated heterochromatin forms positionally and mechanically stable genomic domains even though the component HP1 paralogs, HP1α, HP1β, and HP1γ, display rapid on-off dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known biological observation that motivates the study.

claim: HP1-mediated heterochromatin forms positionally and mechanically stable genomic domains in mammals.
source: In mammals, HP1-mediated heterochromatin forms positionally and mechanically stable genomic domains even though the component HP1 paralogs, HP1α, HP1β, and HP1γ, display rapid on-off dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known biological observation.

claim: Within phase-separated HP1α-DNA condensates, HP1α acts as a dynamic liquid.
source: Using bulk and single-molecule methods, we show that, within phase-separated HP1α-DNA condensates, HP1α acts as a dynamic liquid, while compacted DNA molecules are constrained in local territories.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Compacted DNA molecules are constrained in local territories within HP1α-DNA condensates.
source: Using bulk and single-molecule methods, we show that, within phase-separated HP1α-DNA condensates, HP1α acts as a dynamic liquid, while compacted DNA molecules are constrained in local territories.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated by DNA mixing experiments in Figure 3E.

claim: HP1α-DNA condensates are resistant to large forces.
source: These condensates are resistant to large forces yet can be readily dissolved by HP1β.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by optical trapping experiments in Figure 4.

claim: HP1α-DNA condensates can be readily dissolved by HP1β.
source: These condensates are resistant to large forces yet can be readily dissolved by HP1β.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by competition experiments in Figure 8B.

claim: Differences in each HP1 paralog's DNA compaction and phase-separation properties arise from their respective disordered regions.
source: Finally, we find that differences in each HP1 paralog's DNA compaction and phase-separation properties arise from their respective disordered regions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by domain swap experiments in Figure 7H-I.

claim: HP1α binds DNA globally along the DNA molecule.
source: Surprisingly, we found that HP1α binds uniformly along DNA, incorporating into both the compacted and uncompacted regions (Figure 1E–L).
evidence: This is a finding from the DNA curtain experiments shown in Figure 1E-L.

claim: HP1α compacts DNA locally at the free end of the DNA molecule.
source: We validated that compaction occurs at the free end by labeling the untethered end of the DNA with a fluorescent dCas9 (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the DNA curtain experiments with dCas9 labeling in Figure 1C-E.

claim: HP1α incorporates into compacted DNA at the same rate as on uncompacted DNA at 50 μM HP1α.
source: And by comparison, we found that HP1α incorporates into compacted DNA at the same rate as on uncompacted DNA at 50 μM HP1α, and moderately faster into the compacted DNA at 5 μM HP1α (Figure 1J–L).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the DNA curtain experiments shown in Figure 1J-L.

claim: HP1α incorporates into compacted DNA moderately faster than uncompacted DNA at 5 μM HP1α.
source: And by comparison, we found that HP1α incorporates into compacted DNA at the same rate as on uncompacted DNA at 50 μM HP1α, and moderately faster into the compacted DNA at 5 μM HP1α (Figure 1J–L).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the DNA curtain experiments shown in Figure 1J-L.

claim: Compacted DNA states continue to support ingress and egress of HP1α from solution.
source: We conclude that compacted DNA states are not inaccessibly compacted, but rather continue to support ingress and egress of HP1α from solution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that HP1α continues to bind to compacted DNA regions.

claim: HP1α compacts DNA at a rate of 47 kbp/s at 50 μM concentration.
source: Indeed, the rapid and constant speed of DNA compaction against buffer flow (47 kbp/s at <1 pN for 50 μM HP1α) suggests that HP1α capitalizes upon DNA fluctuations that bring linearly distal segments of DNA together (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Baumann et al., 2000; Ostrovsky and Bar-Yam, 1994).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the DNA curtain experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HP1α capitalizes upon DNA fluctuations that bring linearly distal segments of DNA together during compaction.
source: Indeed, the rapid and constant speed of DNA compaction against buffer flow (47 kbp/s at <1 pN for 50 μM HP1α) suggests that HP1α capitalizes upon DNA fluctuations that bring linearly distal segments of DNA together (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Baumann et al., 2000; Ostrovsky and Bar-Yam, 1994).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the compaction data supported by citations to polymer physics literature.

claim: The initiation of DNA compaction by HP1α is localized to the untethered end of the DNA due to lower tension allowing for more DNA conformations.
source: Such a model then explains why the initiation of compaction is localized to the untethered end of the DNA: the lower tension at the untethered end allows for a larger number of DNA conformations that bring distal regions of the DNA into close proximity.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the observed localization of compaction initiation.

claim: HP1α remains soluble at concentrations up to 400 μM in 70 mM KCl buffer.
source: At the conditions these experiments were performed (70 mM KCl, 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 1 mM DTT), HP1α remains soluble even at exceedingly high concentrations (400 μM) (Figure 2A, bottom right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phase diagram in Figure 2A showing no condensates at 400 μM HP1α without DNA.

claim: HP1α readily condenses into liquid phase-separated material in the presence of DNA.
source: However, in the presence of DNA, HP1α readily condenses into concentrated liquid phase-separated material (Figure 2A) indicating the formation of a network of weak interactions interconnecting HP1α and DNA molecules.
evidence: This is shown by the phase diagram in Figure 2A demonstrating condensate formation with DNA.

claim: The critical concentration of HP1α necessary to induce phase separation with 147 bp DNA is approximately 50 μM.
source: First, we estimated the critical concentration of HP1α necessary to induce phase separation to be ~50 µM in the presence of 147 bp DNA at concentrations ranging from 0.125 to 4 µM (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is determined from the phase diagram in Figure 2A.

claim: Lowering DNA concentration results in a continuous reduction in the average size of HP1α-DNA condensates rather than a sharp disappearance.
source: However, above this critical concentration of HP1α, we were unable to measure a corresponding critical concentration for DNA. Rather, lowering the DNA concentration resulted in a continuous reduction in the average size of observed HP1α-DNA condensates instead of a sharp disappearance (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by the phase diagram and quantification in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The critical concentration of HP1α is largely invariant of DNA concentration.
source: Thus, we conclude the critical concentration of HP1α is largely invariant of DNA concentration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that condensates form across a wide range of DNA concentrations above the HP1α critical concentration.

claim: HP1α-DNA condensates are observed even at very large ratios of HP1α to DNA (5000:1).
source: In fact, even at very large ratios of HP1α to DNA (5000:1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), we still observe condensates.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The apparent dissociation constant for HP1α interactions with ~60–200 bp DNA ranges from 0.3 to 10 μM.
source: The apparent dissociation constant for HP1α interactions with ~60–200 bp DNA ranges from 0.3 to 10 μM (Nishibuchi et al., 2014; Figure 2—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to prior work and supported by anisotropy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The average droplet size versus concentration of both DNA and HP1α is well described by a power law.
source: We find the average droplet size versus concentration of both DNA and HP1α is in fact well described by a power law (Figure 2C), further connecting the formation of macroscopic liquid droplets to the microscopic processes of aggregation and DNA compaction.
evidence: This is shown by the power law fits in Figure 2C.

claim: At 40 mM KCl, high concentrations (~400 μM) of HP1α can undergo LLPS in the absence of DNA.
source: Notably, at 40 mM KCl, high concentrations (~400 μM) of HP1α can undergo LLPS in the absence of DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Under 75 mM KCl conditions and in the absence of DNA, the critical concentration for HP1α to exhibit LLPS is greater than 800 μM.
source: However, under similar ionic conditions to those used in the bulk of this study (75 mM KCl), and in the absence of DNA, the critical concentration for HP1α to exhibit LLPS is greater than 800 μM, and HP1α predominantly exists as a dimer (Larson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to prior work.

claim: Increasing DNA length from 147 bp to 2.7 kbp results in an order of magnitude decrease in the critical HP1α concentration required to induce LLPS (from 50 μM to 3 μM).
source: Upon increasing the size of linear DNA co-incubated with HP1α from 147 bp to 2.7 kbp, we observed an order of magnitude decrease in the critical HP1α concentration required to induce LLPS (50 μM to 3 μM) (Figure 2A,E).
evidence: This is shown by comparing the phase diagrams in Figure 2A and 2E.

claim: Increasing the DNA length from 2.7 kbp to 9 kbp did not lead to an additional decrease in the critical concentration of HP1α at 70 mM KCl.
source: Conversely, at 70 mM KCl, increasing the DNA length from 2.7 kbp to 9 kbp did not lead to an additional decrease in the critical concentration of HP1α (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E comparing condensate formation with different DNA lengths.

claim: HP1α-induced DNA compaction occurs at concentrations as low as 500 nM on DNA curtains.
source: In our single molecule assay, we observed HP1α-induced DNA compaction at concentrations as low as 500 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: The rate of DNA compaction at 500 nM HP1α was roughly 30 times slower than at 5 µM HP1α.
source: However, the rate of DNA compaction exhibited by 500 nM HP1α was roughly 30 times slower than the compaction rate at 5 µM HP1α where we might have predicted only a 10 times slower rate of compaction based on an expected change in the pseudo-first order association rate constant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of compaction rates shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HP1α-DNA condensates formed with 147 bp DNA rapidly coalesce into spherical structures immediately following fusion.
source: HP1α-DNA condensates formed with 147 bp DNA rapidly coalesce into spherical structures immediately following fusion (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in the time-lapse images in Figure 2D.

claim: Increasing the DNA length to 2.7 kbp substantially (>100 times) lengthens the time required for coalescence of HP1α-DNA condensates.
source: However, increasing the DNA length to 2.7 kbp substantially (>100 times) lengthens the time required for coalescence (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown by comparing coalescence times in Figure 2D for different DNA lengths.

claim: Condensates formed with 9 kbp DNA were unable to complete coalescence within an hour.
source: Moreover, condensates formed with 9 kbp DNA (~60X larger than 147 bp) were unable to complete coalescence within an hour (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in the time-lapse images in Figure 2D.

claim: The rate of HP1α recovery in condensates is unaffected by changes in DNA length after partial photobleaching.
source: We find that for HP1α, despite large differences in droplet morphology, the rate of recovery is unaffected by changes in DNA length after partial photobleaching (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is shown by the FRAP experiments in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Condensates formed with DNA ranging in length from 147 bp to ~50 kbp showed recovery of HP1α fluorescence with comparable t1/2 values (~2 s).
source: Condensates formed with DNA ranging in length from 147 bp to ~50 kbp showed recovery of fluorescence with comparable t1/2 values (~2 s) (Figure 3C), which are strikingly similar to recovery rates of HP1α measured in vivo (Cheutin et al., 2003; Festenstein et al., 2003).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and compared to in vivo measurements from cited literature.

claim: HP1α recovery rates in vitro (~2 s) are strikingly similar to recovery rates of HP1α measured in vivo.
source: Condensates formed with DNA ranging in length from 147 bp to ~50 kbp showed recovery of fluorescence with comparable t1/2 values (~2 s) (Figure 3C), which are strikingly similar to recovery rates of HP1α measured in vivo (Cheutin et al., 2003; Festenstein et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison to in vivo data from cited literature.

claim: HP1α readily exchanges within condensates and between condensate and solution populations without disruption of the condensates.
source: These results demonstrate that HP1α readily exchanges within condensates, and between condensate and solution populations, without disruption of the condensates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP and mixing experiments.

claim: Within seconds after mixing, both HP1α−488 and HP1α−565 partitioned equally into all droplets.
source: Within seconds after mixing, both HP1α−488 and HP1α−565 were found to have partitioned equally into all droplets (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is shown in the two-color mixing experiments in Figure 3D.

claim: DNA does not rapidly mix across condensates after fusion but is instead maintained in large and long lived (>1 hr) single-color sub-condensate domains.
source: Contrary to the observations above, DNA does not rapidly mix across condensates after fusion but is instead maintained in large and long lived (>1 hr) single-color sub-condensate domains (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is shown in the two-color DNA mixing experiments in Figure 3E.

claim: FRAP experiments of HP1α-DNA condensates labeled with YOYO-1 exhibit recovery rates proportional to DNA length: the longer the DNA, the slower the rate of recovery.
source: Furthermore, FRAP experiments of HP1α-DNA condensates labeled with YOYO-1 exhibit recovery rates proportional to DNA length: the longer the DNA, the slower the rate of recovery (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Digestion of DNA with MNase results in rapid coalescence and mixing of alternately labeled DNA within condensates.
source: Digestion of the DNA reveals this expectation to be accurate, and we observe rapid coalescence and mixing of alternately labeled DNA within condensates (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in the MNase treatment experiments in Figure 3F.

claim: Sequestered DNA domains measuring on average 10 kbp are able to resist disruption to an instantaneous force of 40pN.
source: From this measurement, we identify three prominent features of HP1α-DNA interactions. First, sequestered DNA domains, measuring on average 10 kbp, are able to resist disruption to an instantaneous force of 40pN (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is shown in the optical trapping experiments in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Smaller HP1α-DNA structures (~1–2 kbps) rupture at lower forces ranging from 5 to 20pN.
source: However, smaller HP1α-DNA structures (~1–2 kbps) are observed to rupture at lower forces ranging from 5 to 20pN, suggesting the stability of HP1α-compacted DNA scales by size (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, see '*').
evidence: This is shown in the optical trapping experiments in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The stability of HP1α-compacted DNA scales by size.
source: However, smaller HP1α-DNA structures (~1–2 kbps) are observed to rupture at lower forces ranging from 5 to 20pN, suggesting the stability of HP1α-compacted DNA scales by size (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, see '*').
evidence: This is an interpretation of the force-dependent rupture data.

claim: An average energetic barrier of ~1 kbT/bp of compacted DNA separates HP1α-compacted states of DNA from extended DNA states in the absence of HP1α.
source: Second, by integrating the area between the force-extension curves for DNA alone and in the presence of HP1α, we estimate that an average energetic barrier of ~1 kbT/bp of compacted DNA separates HP1α-compacted states of DNA from extended DNA states in the absence of HP1α (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is calculated from the force-extension curves in Figure 4C.

claim: Each successive stretch-relax cycle resulted in more DNA stably sequestered by HP1α.
source: Finally, we observed that each successive SRC resulted in more DNA stably sequestered by HP1α (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in the optical trapping experiments in Figure 4C.

claim: After HP1α-DNA condensates are subjected to strain, polymer rearrangements and/or force-dependent selection of HP1α-binding interactions provide a basis for further stable compaction of DNA by HP1α.
source: This surprising result shows that, after HP1α-DNA condensates are subjected to strain, polymer rearrangements and/or force-dependent selection of HP1α-binding interactions provide a basis for further stable compaction of DNA by HP1α.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that successive stretch-relax cycles increase compaction.

claim: During the waiting period after relaxation, a steady force increase over time is observed in HP1α-DNA condensates.
source: During the waiting period after relaxation, we observe a steady force increase over time (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is shown in the optical trapping experiments with waiting periods in Figure 4E.

claim: Even in the absence of free HP1α, the population of already bound HP1α molecules is sufficient to induce compaction in the low force regime (~1 pN).
source: We find that even in the absence of free HP1α, the population of already bound HP1α molecules is sufficient to induce compaction in the low force regime (~1 pN) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the optical trapping experiments without free protein in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: When DNA is held at a steady extension following stretching, a drop in measured force over time is observed, indicating that HP1α-DNA condensates are biased toward disassembly during sustained higher forces.
source: When the DNA is held at a steady extension of 15.5 μm following stretching, we observe a drop in measured force over time (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E). This relaxation indicates that HP1α-DNA condensates are biased toward disassembly during sustained higher forces.
evidence: This is shown in the optical trapping experiments in Figure 4F.

claim: The disassembly of HP1α-DNA condensates at higher forces proceeds at the same rate irrespective of the presence of HP1α in solution.
source: We find that the disassembly of HP1α-DNA condensates at higher forces proceeds at the same rate irrespective of the presence of HP1α in solution (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by comparing disassembly rates with and without free protein in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The hinge domain of HP1α is sufficient for DNA compaction.
source: Surprisingly, not only is the hinge domain sufficient for DNA compaction (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C), but also compaction proceeds at twice speed of the full-length protein (Figure 5C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the DNA curtain experiments with the hinge domain in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The hinge domain of HP1α compacts DNA at twice the speed of the full-length protein.
source: Surprisingly, not only is the hinge domain sufficient for DNA compaction (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C), but also compaction proceeds at twice speed of the full-length protein (Figure 5C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by comparing compaction rates in Figure 5C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The hinge domain of HP1α is sufficient to induce the formation of condensates with DNA.
source: Additionally, the hinge domain is sufficient to induce the formation of condensates with DNA (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is shown in the phase separation assays in Figure 5D-E.

claim: With short (147 bp) DNA oligomers, the critical concentration for condensate formation by the hinge domain is reduced by a factor of four relative to full-length HP1α (from 50 to 12.5 μM).
source: And, even with short (147 bp) DNA oligomers, the critical concentration for condensate formation is reduced by a factor of four relative to full-length HP1α (from 50 to 12.5 μM) (Figures 2A and 5D).
evidence: This is shown by comparing the phase diagrams in Figures 2A and 5D.

claim: Removal of the NTE (HP1α-ΔNTE) abolished detectable condensate formation with short DNA oligomers.
source: Removal of the NTE (HP1α-ΔNTE) abolished detectable condensate formation with short DNA oligomers and increased the critical concentration for condensate formation with longer DNA (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is shown in the phase separation assays in Figure 6A-B.

claim: HP1α-ΔNTE compacted DNA ~20 times slower than full-length HP1α and only managed to compact ~7 kbp of the available ~50 kbps.
source: Furthermore, HP1α-ΔNTE compacted DNA ~20 times slower than full-length HP1α and only managed to compact ~7 kbp of the available ~50 kbps (Figure 6C,E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is shown in the DNA curtain experiments in Figure 6C,E.

claim: Deletion of the CTE (HP1α-ΔCTE) decreased the critical concentration for condensation with 147 bp DNA oligomers an order of magnitude.
source: In contrast, deletion of the CTE (HP1α-ΔCTE) decreased the critical concentration for condensation with 147 bp DNA oligomers an order of magnitude (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is shown in the phase separation assays in Figure 6A-B.

claim: HP1α-ΔCTE compacted DNA three times faster than full-length HP1α and almost twice the apparent rate measured for the hinge domain alone.
source: HP1α-ΔCTE also compacted DNA three times faster than full-length HP1α and almost twice the apparent rate measured for the hinge domain alone (Figure 6C–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown by comparing compaction rates in Figure 6C-D.

claim: The CTE negatively regulates the activity of the hinge domain in the context of full-length HP1α.
source: Together with the compaction activity of the hinge and HP1α-ΔCTE, these data demonstrate that the CTE negatively regulates the activity of the hinge domain in the context of full-length HP1α.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the domain deletion experiments.

claim: HP1β displays a substantially reduced rate of DNA compaction relative to HP1α.
source: We find that HP1β displays a substantially reduced rate of DNA compaction relative to HP1α (Figure 7C,E).
evidence: This is shown in the DNA curtain experiments comparing HP1β and HP1α in Figure 7C,E.

claim: Despite slower compaction, HP1β continues to sustain compacted DNA even after the bulk of the injected pulse of HP1β has passed through the flowcell.
source: Yet, despite slower compaction, HP1β continues to sustain compacted DNA even after the bulk of the injected pulse of HP1β has passed through the flowcell (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is shown in the DNA curtain experiments in Figure 7E.

claim: HP1γ compacts DNA more rapidly than HP1β, although HP1γ does not achieve the rapid compaction rates of HP1α.
source: In comparison, HP1γ compacts DNA more rapidly than HP1β, although HP1γ does not achieve the rapid compaction rates of HP1α (Figure 7D–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is shown in the DNA curtain experiments comparing the three paralogs in Figure 7D-E.

claim: HP1γ rapidly disassembles as the concentration of free HP1γ in the flowcell begins to decline.
source: Moreover, HP1γ rapidly disassembles as the concentration of free HP1γ in the flowcell begins to decline (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is shown in the DNA curtain experiments in Figure 7E.

claim: HP1γ forms condensates with 3 kbp DNA, although the critical HP1γ concentration required to induce droplet formation is higher than that for HP1α.
source: We find that HP1γ does form condensates with 3 kbp DNA, although the critical HP1γ concentration required to induce droplet formation is, in fact, higher than that for HP1α (Figure 2E, Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown in the phase separation assays in Figure 7F.

claim: HP1γ does not form condensates with 147 bp DNA under conditions where HP1α continues to drive DNA condensation.
source: Moreover, HP1γ does not form condensates with 147 bp DNA, under conditions where HP1α continues to drive DNA condensation (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is shown in the phase separation assays in Figure 7G.

claim: HP1β does not induce droplet formation regardless of the length of co-incubated DNA.
source: In contrast, we find that HP1β does not induce droplet formation regardless of the length of co-incubated DNA (Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the phase separation assays in Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Both HP1α-βhinge and HP1α-γhinge mutants fail to produce condensates in the presence of DNA.
source: We find that both mutants fail to produce condensates in the presence of DNA (Figure 7I), demonstrating that, within the context of full-length HP1α and the HP1 paralogs, the HP1α's hinge domain is necessary for droplet formation.
evidence: This is shown in the phase separation assays with hinge swap mutants in Figure 7I.

claim: Within the context of full-length HP1α and the HP1 paralogs, the HP1α's hinge domain is necessary for droplet formation.
source: We find that both mutants fail to produce condensates in the presence of DNA (Figure 7I), demonstrating that, within the context of full-length HP1α and the HP1 paralogs, the HP1α's hinge domain is necessary for droplet formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the hinge swap experiments.

claim: Both HP1β-αhinge and HP1γ-αhinge mutants readily form condensates with DNA.
source: We find both these mutants now readily form condensates with DNA, demonstrating the HP1α hinge is also sufficient for phase separation in the context of the other HP1 paralogs (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is shown in the phase separation assays with hinge swap mutants in Figure 7I.

claim: The HP1α hinge is sufficient for phase separation in the context of the other HP1 paralogs.
source: We find both these mutants now readily form condensates with DNA, demonstrating the HP1α hinge is also sufficient for phase separation in the context of the other HP1 paralogs (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the hinge swap experiments.

claim: The critical concentration for condensate formation was two-times lower for HP1β-αhinge and ten-times lower for HP1γ-αhinge than for HP1α.
source: Intriguingly, the critical concentration for condensate formation was decidedly lower for both α-hinge mutants than for HP1α; two-times lower for HP1β-αhinge and ten-times lower for HP1γ-αhinge (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is shown in the phase separation assays in Figure 7I.

claim: The HP1α hinge is more active outside of its native context where it is free from the inhibitory effect of its CTE.
source: These results indicate that the HP1α hinge is more active outside of its native context where it is free from the inhibitory effect of its CTE.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hinge swap results.

claim: When HP1β or HP1γ were premixed with HP1α and added to DNA, both HP1β and HP1γ inhibited droplet formation in a concentration-dependent fashion.
source: When HP1β or HP1γ were premixed with HP1α and added to DNA to assess condensate formation, both HP1β and HP1γ inhibited droplet formation in a concentration-dependent fashion (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is shown in the competition assays in Figure 8A.

claim: When introduced to pre-formed HP1α-DNA condensates, HP1β is capable of invading and subsequently dissolving condensates at a rate proportional to HP1α exchange.
source: Interestingly, when introduced to pre-formed HP1α-DNA condensates, HP1β is capable of invading and subsequently dissolving condensates at a rate proportional to HP1α exchange (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is shown in the competition assays in Figure 8B.

claim: HP1γ does not destabilize pre-formed HP1α-DNA condensates, but rather enriches in them.
source: In contrast, HP1γ does not destabilize, but rather enriches in the pre-formed HP1α-DNA condensates (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown in the competition assays in Figure 8C.

claim: Heterochromatin domains are typically found to be statically positioned within the nucleus for several hours.
source: Heterochromatin domains are typically found to be statically positioned within the nucleus for several hours, held separate from euchromatin (Gerlich et al., 2003; Marshall et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: Heterochromatin domains can be rapidly disassembled in response to environmental and developmental cues.
source: Yet, these domains can also be rapidly disassembled in response to environmental and developmental cues (Cheutin and Cavalli, 2012; Dion and Gasser, 2013; Kind et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: HP1 molecules in heterochromatin domains exchange within seconds.
source: The finding that HP1 molecules in these domains exchange within seconds provides some insight into how these domains can be dissolved, because competing molecules would be able to rapidly displace HP1 proteins from DNA (Cheutin et al., 2003; Festenstein et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: HP1α is mostly associated with gene repression and chromosome segregation.
source: For example, HP1α is mostly associated with gene repression and chromosome segregation (Allshire and Madhani, 2018; Canzio et al., 2014; Eissenberg and Elgin, 2014)
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: HP1β plays both gene activating and gene repressive roles.
source: HP1β plays both gene activating and gene repressive roles (Allshire and Madhani, 2018; Canzio et al., 2014; Eissenberg and Elgin, 2014)
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: HP1γ is more often associated with promoting transcription.
source: and HP1γ is more often associated with promoting transcription (Allshire and Madhani, 2018; Canzio et al., 2014; Eissenberg and Elgin, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: HP1 proteins are sufficient to bind to DNA and chromatin and to provoke their robust condensation.
source: For example, it has been shown that HP1 proteins are sufficient to bind to DNA and chromatin and to provoke their robust condensation (Azzaz et al., 2014; Canzio et al., 2011; Kilic et al., 2018; Kilic et al., 2015; Larson et al., 2017; Meehan et al., 2003; Mishima et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: HP1 molecules exhibit weak affinity for chromatin in vitro.
source: Furthermore, and consistent with cellular measurements, HP1 molecules also exhibit weak affinity for chromatin in vitro (Canzio et al., 2013; Canzio et al., 2011; Kilic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: The human HP1 protein, HP1α was shown to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro when phosphorylated and in combination with DNA.
source: Specifically, the human HP1 protein, HP1α was shown to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro when phosphorylated and in combination with DNA (Larson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation to prior work.

claim: The Drosophila HP1 protein, HP1a, forms phase-separated condensates in vivo.
source: Parallel studies showed that the Drosophila HP1 protein, HP1a, also forms phase-separated condensates in vivo (Strom et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation to prior work.

claim: HP1β cannot undergo LLPS in vitro upon phosphorylation or in combination with DNA.
source: In contrast, HP1β cannot undergo LLPS in vitro upon phosphorylation or in combination with DNA, but can be recruited to liquid phases of modified chromatin (Larson et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: HP1β can be recruited to liquid phases of modified chromatin.
source: In contrast, HP1β cannot undergo LLPS in vitro upon phosphorylation or in combination with DNA, but can be recruited to liquid phases of modified chromatin (Larson et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: A recent study has implied that HP1-mediated heterochromatin in cells does not exhibit liquid-like phase-separated behavior.
source: A recent study has implied that HP1-mediated heterochromatin in cells does not exhibit liquid-like phase-separated behavior (Erdel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as background with citation to prior work.

claim: The chromodomain (CD) of HP1α binds to di- and tri-methylation of lysine 9 on histone 3 (H3K9me).
source: The CD binds to di- and tri-methylation of lysine 9 on histone 3 (H3K9me) and the CSD mediates HP1 dimerization as well as interactions with other nuclear proteins (Canzio et al., 2011; Eissenberg et al., 1990; Kaustov et al., 2011; Smothers and Henikoff, 2000).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: The chromoshadow domain (CSD) of HP1α mediates HP1 dimerization as well as interactions with other nuclear proteins.
source: The CD binds to di- and tri-methylation of lysine 9 on histone 3 (H3K9me) and the CSD mediates HP1 dimerization as well as interactions with other nuclear proteins (Canzio et al., 2011; Eissenberg et al., 1990; Kaustov et al., 2011; Smothers and Henikoff, 2000).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: The central disordered region, or hinge domain, of HP1α mediates DNA binding.
source: The central disordered region, or hinge domain, of HP1α mediates DNA binding (Meehan et al., 2003; Smothers and Henikoff, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: The N-terminal extension (NTE) and the C-terminal extension (CTE) of HP1α have been shown to regulate oligomerization of phosphorylated HP1α.
source: Finally, the N-terminal extension (NTE) and the C-terminal extension (CTE) of HP1α have been shown to regulate oligomerization of phosphorylated HP1α (Larson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation to prior work.

claim: Cellular localization of HP1α at heterochromatic sites is completely abolished by mutations to the hinge domain.
source: While all five domains of HP1α collaborate to determine in vivo localization, cellular localization at heterochromatic sites is completely abolished by mutations to the hinge domain of HP1α (Cheutin et al., 2003; Kellum et al., 1995; Yuan and O'Farrell, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.
